dataset_family: ADNI (ADNI-1/GO/2; EMCI subset: 383 patients with clinical data, of whom 90 had DTI)
method_family: Weighted late-fusion ensemble: a random forest on 9 clinical/EHR features and a NASNet CNN on single-slice DTI (ADC), with probability weights chosen by grid search. Close to P-81's family (CNN imaging branch late-fused with cognitive data).
what_it_shows: Within one ADNI EMCI sample, the weighted RF (clinical) + CNN (DTI) ensemble reports 98.81% accuracy (AUC .992), against 96.43% (AUC .973) for the DTI-only CNN and 92.86% (AUC .960) for the clinical-only RF (Tables 5, 6 and 8; text p.6). The ensemble weight (0.55 CNN / 0.45 RF) is the highest-accuracy run of a grid over weights. In the same Table 5, the ensemble at equal weights scores 95.24%, below DTI alone; at 0.40/0.60 it scores 94.05%; and at 0.70/0.30 and 0.65/0.35 it ties DTI alone at 96.43%.
why: PDF identity: the title, authors (Velazquez and Lee, UMKC), journal and DOI 10.1016/j.compbiomed.2022.106201 match the P-1 block, whose header is only the filename. The study does run the head-to-head in the form of both wordings. It pits a fused model against each unimodal model, and the 'clinical' branch contains cognitive scores (ADAS11/13, MMSE, FAQ), age, race and APOE4. That branch ALSO contains MRI-derived hippocampal and ventricular volumes (Table 1, p.4), so it is not purely non-imaging. The gain over the imaging model alone (DTI 96.43% to ensemble 98.81%) is what the narrowed wording describes. The stated form also holds as reported, since the ensemble beats both single-source models. I nonetheless answer 'partly' on both, because the comparison is not a fair demonstration. (1) The fusion weight was selected as 'the highest accuracy run' of the grid (p.5), and no separate validation set is described for that choice, so the fused arm got a selection advantage that the unimodal arms did not. The paper's own Table 5 shows that the advantage over DTI alone appears at only 2 of 6 mixed weights, ties at 2, and reverses at 2, including the equal 0.50/0.50 weighting (95.24% vs 96.43%). (2) The margins are tiny. By my arithmetic, not stated in the paper, 98.81%, 96.43% and 92.86% correspond to 83, 81 and 78 correct of 84 cases. The paper does not describe how an 84-case ensemble evaluation set was assembled, when only 90 patients had DTI and the RF and CNN used different test splits (25% of clinical data; 10% of images, p.6). (3) There is a leakage risk. Table 4 (p.6) lists the 'Testing Data' as oversampled/augmented records (402/402 clinical records; 144,000/666,000 images), which implies that oversampling and augmentation preceded the split. The authors also report repeating and tuning each model 'several dozen times' against its performance (pp.6-7). (4) Accuracy is the only metric for the weight grid; there are no significance tests and no external test; the population is EMCI; and conversion is 'eventual', defined at the last exam, with a variable horizon. Independence: the data are ADNI, the same dataset family as all three current supporters and as P-211, so the paper adds no dataset-family independence. The method (CNN imaging branch plus late fusion with cognitive data) is near P-81's family. No shared authors with P-3 (Luo, He, Cui, Chen, Ward), P-104 (Shen, Zhu, Zhang, Wang, Chen, Xu, Shao) or P-81 (Cao, Ma, Nayak, Duong). Peer-reviewed journal article, not a preprint.

quotes.quote: When both modalities (clinical data and DTI scans) are provided, our weighted ensemble model achieves an EMCI-to-AD conversion prediction accuracy of 98.81%. With only clinical data being supplied, our model maintains an accuracy of 92.86%. When only DTI scans are provided, our model performs at 96.43% accuracy.
Once the grid search has been completed, the weights of the highest accuracy run (0.55 CNN, 0.45 RF) are captured and used for the final ensemble model.

As the model spent significant time being fine-tuned, the experiment was repeated several dozen times per model. After each repeat, performance metrics were assessed to see how to tune the model further.

These features contained physical biomarkers (ventricular and hippocampal volume), genetic biomarkers (APOE4), neuropsychological scale scores (FAQ, MMSE, ADAS13, ADAS11), and demographic variables (age, race).
A limitation of our study is that all patients were derived from the ADNI data set.
